a: brothers
p: Paul's word is the plural 'brothers' (adelphoi), which Greek used for a whole group, women included.
b: The Greek adelphoi is the masculine plural, and Greek used it for a mixed group. Paul means every member of the house churches in Rome, as chapter 16 shows: he calls Phoebe "our sister" (16:1) and greets Prisca, Junia, Mary and others by name. See the note at Romans 1:13 for the same choice. This site renders it "brothers" everywhere, as in Acts, where the same plural is used of mixed groups (Acts 1:15, among a company that included the women named in Acts 1:14; Acts 21:17; Acts 28:14). Here too the hearers are plainly men and women together. The English "brothers" is a translation choice, not a limit on whom Paul addresses. The word also carries Paul's tone: he is not commanding as an apostle over the church but appealing as a relative. The "therefore" that begins the verse looks back over all of chapters 1 to 11, and "God's compassion" most directly to the mercy to Jews and Gentiles in 11:30-32.
r: Romans 1:13; Romans 11:30; Romans 16:1; Romans 16:14; Acts 1:15; Acts 21:17; Acts 28:14

a: a sacrifice that is alive, holy and welcome to God
p: Paul uses the vocabulary of the temple for what believers do with their bodies.
b: "Sacrifice," "holy" and "welcome" (the Greek euarestos, used in the Greek Old Testament for what pleases God at the altar) are all offering words (Leviticus 1:3-4). Paul turns them around. The animal on the altar was killed; this sacrifice is "alive." And the "bodies" are not just flesh but whole persons, with their hands, work, money and relationships, which is why the rest of the chapter is about how people treat each other. Paul will describe his own work in the same terms at 15:16. The prophets had already taught that God wants obedience more than animals (Psalm 40:6-8; Hosea 6:6), and Hebrews 13:15-16 and 1 Peter 2:5 use the same idea.
r: Leviticus 1:3; Psalm 40:6; Hosea 6:6; Romans 15:16; Hebrews 13:15; 1 Peter 2:5

a: sensible worship
p: The Greek logikos has been translated 'reasonable', 'spiritual' and 'rational'.
b: The phrase is logikē latreia. Latreia means service to God, especially worship. Logikos comes from logos (word, reason) and has several possible senses. (1) "Sensible" or "rational": worship fitting for beings who think, as opposed to animal sacrifice. The Stoics and some Greek texts spoke of "rational sacrifices" in this way, and 1 Peter 2:2 uses the same adjective. (2) "Spiritual," as the Latin Vulgate's rationabile was often read, set against outward ritual. (3) "According to the Word," worship shaped by God's word. (4) "Logical," the reasonable response to the mercies of chapters 1 to 11. Commentators weigh all four; the first two are the most common. The Plain follows the plainest sense in 8th-grade English.

a: Stop shaping yourselves to fit this age.
p: Paul contrasts 'this age' with a renewed mind; the verb for 'transformed' is the one used of Jesus' transfiguration.
b: "This age" (aiōn) is the present era, which Jewish writers of Paul's time called the evil age that God would end (Galatians 1:4). The verb "shape yourselves to fit" (syschēmatizomai) is about taking on an outward pattern, like wearing a mold. "Be transformed" is metamorphoō, the word used when Jesus was changed in front of three disciples (Mark 9:2) and when Paul says believers are being changed into the Lord's likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18). The change comes through "the renewing of your mind": not a technique but a continuing work of God, since the mind was the thing that had gone wrong in 1:21 and 1:28. The purpose is practical: "to test and prove what God's will is."
r: Galatians 1:4; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Mark 9:2; Romans 1:28; Ephesians 4:23; Colossians 3:10

a: a measure of faith
p: Is faith the standard we judge ourselves by, or the share God gives each person?
b: Paul says God has "handed each of you a measure of faith." Two readings are common. (1) The "measure" is how much faith or gifting God gives each person, so differences between believers are God's doing and give no ground for pride; this fits the gifts in the verses that follow. (2) "Faith" itself is the measure: everyone has the same standard, trust in Christ, and measures themselves by it (C. E. B. Cranfield argues this). Either way the point is the same: Paul warns against thinking of oneself as better than other members, probably with the quarrel of the strong and weak (14:1 to 15:13) in view. The word "faith" is not the doctrines of the church here but trust.

a: A single body has many parts
t: The body as a picture of a community
p: Rome already knew the picture of a body of many parts; Paul gives it a new center in Christ.
b: Greek and Roman writers used the body as an image of a city. Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa, in 494 BC, stopped a revolt by the poor with the story of the belly and the limbs (Livy 2.32), and the story was still told in Paul's day. Paul uses the same picture for a different aim. The body is not a social order where each part keeps its place under the belly; it is "one body in Christ" (12:5), and each part "belongs to the others," so no member is below the rest. He draws the image out at greater length in 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 (not yet written on this site), and Ephesians 4:4-16 uses it again.

a: We have gifts that differ
p: Seven gifts are named; none is a tongue, a healing or a miracle (the kinds listed in 1 Corinthians 12 to 14).
b: The word is charismata, "grace-gifts," from charis (grace). Paul's list here is: prophecy, service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leading, and showing mercy. It differs from the lists in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10 and 12:28 and Ephesians 4:11 (not all of these are written on this site yet), so it is clearly an example, not a full count. It names no tongues, healing or miracles, though prophecy is on the list, and every item is something that can be done in an ordinary house church. The gifts come "by the grace given to us," and Paul says the same of his own work (12:3). The churches differ on whether the gifts of prophecy and healing still occur today; see the card below.

a: in line with the proportion of faith
p: Paul probably means 'in proportion to your faith', not the later Protestant rule of reading Scripture by Scripture.
b: The Greek kata tēn analogian tēs pisteōs gave English the phrase "analogy of faith." Two meanings have been drawn from it. (1) The older reading in the West: prophecy must agree with the body of Christian belief ("the faith"), and from this later writers took the rule that Scripture is explained by Scripture. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (114) also uses "analogy of faith" for the coherence of the truths of the faith. (2) Most modern commentators: each prophet should speak in proportion to the faith God gave that person (12:3), without going beyond it. Paul elsewhere says prophecy must be tested (1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21).

a: If it is service, let it be used in serving.
t: Service, the word behind Phoebe's title
p: The Greek for 'service' and 'servant' is the same root as Phoebe's title in 16:1.
b: Diakonia is the common Greek word for service, and a diakonos is one who serves. Paul uses the same root for his own work (11:13; 15:31), for Christ ("a servant of the circumcised," 15:8), for the governing authority (13:4), and for Phoebe (16:1). Later the church used the word for an office, the deacon. Whether Paul means a defined role here is not clear; the verse speaks of an activity, "in serving." See the note at 16:1.

a: The one who leads
t: 'The one who leads' or 'the one who cares for others'
p: The Greek proistamenos can mean to lead or to look after, and shares a root with 'patron' in 16:2.
b: Proistamenos means literally "the one who stands in front." In Greek it covered two jobs: to preside over and to look after, protect or give aid. It is in the list between "gives" and "shows mercy," and it is the root from which prostatis, "patron," comes in 16:2. Many commentators (Dunn, Jewett) therefore think Paul means people who use their influence or resources on behalf of others, as householders who hosted churches did. Others keep the usual "leads." The Plain follows the common sense; the other is real. 1 Thessalonians 5:12 uses the same verb of those who "have charge of you in the Lord."

a: The one who gives, with generosity.
p: The Greek haplotes means single-heartedness, and so open-handed giving.
b: Haplotēs is literally "simplicity," a heart not divided or looking for a return. In Paul's other letters it is the word for the generosity of the Macedonian churches (2 Corinthians 8:2) and of the Corinthians' gift (2 Corinthians 9:11, 13). The verb "gives" (metadidōmi) means to share what one has. Some commentators think Paul has in mind the wealthier householders of the church, since the next phrase also fits people with authority and means; others see ordinary members sharing. Either way, the manner (open, not showy) matters as much as the act.

a: Let love be real, with no acting.
p: The Greek anypokritos is the opposite of the word for a stage actor, hypocrite.
b: Anypokritos is "without hypocrisy," and a hypokritēs was a stage actor (see the note on "hypocrite" in Matthew 6:2). Love that is real is love that does not play a part. The next twelve verses (12:9-21) are a string of short commands, in the style Jews and Greeks called advice for living, and many echo the teaching of Jesus (Matthew 5:38-48; Luke 6:27-36) and the book of Proverbs. They are not arranged by topic; the thread running through them is love in the church (12:9-13), love toward those outside who hurt it (12:14-21).

a: Be slaves of the Lord.
t: 'Serve the Lord' is 'be slaves of the Lord'
p: Paul's verb is the verb for being a slave; a variant has 'serving the time'.
b: The Greek douleuontes is the verb that goes with doulos, "slave," the word with which Paul begins the letter (1:1). The usual English "serve the Lord" softens it. In 6:22 and 14:18 the same family of words describes the believer's relation to God and Christ. A group of Western manuscripts reads kairō ("the time" or "the moment") instead of kyriō ("the Lord"): "serving the time." Origen's commentary (in Rufinus' Latin) mentions copies with it, so it was in circulation early. See the textual note. The line before it, "Be boiling in spirit," can mean the Holy Spirit or the person's own spirit; see the gloss.

a: Share in the needs of the saints.
t: Sharing with the saints, and hospitality to strangers
p: The verb is the one used for the collection for Jerusalem, and the hospitality is for travelers like Phoebe.
b: "Saints" is Paul's usual word for believers (God's holy people). The verb koinōneō belongs to the family of koinōnia, the word Paul uses for the Jerusalem collection (15:26). Hospitality was a practical need: inns in the Roman world were dirty and unsafe, and traveling Christians, such as teachers, couriers and Phoebe herself (16:1-2), depended on believers' homes. The Greek philoxenia is "love of strangers." Note "chase after," a verb Paul uses for the pursuit of peace in 14:19. Hebrews 13:2 and 1 Peter 4:9 give the same advice.

a: Bless your persecutors.
p: Paul does not say 'Jesus said', but this line matches the Sermon on the Mount and the Sermon on the Plain.
b: Jesus told his followers: "keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44), and "Bless the ones who curse you" (Luke 6:28). Paul does not say these are sayings of Jesus, but scholars (Michael Thompson, James Dunn) have counted a number of close echoes in 12:14-21 and 13:8-10 and hold that Paul and the Romans knew the teaching. Peter gives the same teaching (1 Peter 3:9). The word "persecutors" fits the church's real experience: Jews and Christians had been expelled from Rome within living memory, and Paul himself had been beaten and jailed.

a: go along with the lowly
p: The Greek can mean 'be carried along with humble people' or 'give in to humble tasks'.
b: The verb synapagomenoi means "being led away along with," and the dative tois tapeinois can be masculine ("the lowly," meaning people) or neuter ("lowly things," meaning menial matters). Most commentators take it as people: do not keep to the company of the high and powerful but go along with those of low standing. This fits a church that had slaves, freed people and the poor beside householders (see the greeting list in chapter 16). The neuter reading ("be drawn into humble tasks") is possible. The Plain keeps the plain and probable sense. The next line borrows Proverbs 3:7: "Do not be wise in your own eyes."

a: Take thought for what is honorable in the eyes of all people.
p: Paul's wording follows the Greek of Proverbs 3:4.
b: Proverbs 3:4 in the Septuagint reads "take thought for what is honorable before the Lord and before people," and the Hebrew says you will find favor "in the eyes of God and of people" (Proverbs 3:4). Paul quotes the Greek clause and drops "before the Lord." The concern is public reputation: Christians in Rome were a small group, some of them Jewish and recently allowed back, with a reputation to guard (compare 13:3 and 1 Peter 2:12).

a: make room for the anger
p: Paul writes 'the anger'; nearly all take it as God's, at the last judgment.
b: The Greek is dote topon tē orgē, "give a place to the anger," with no "God's" in the text. Readings: (1) God's anger, in the day of judgment (the common view; Cranfield, Moo). This matches the quotation that follows ("Vengeance is mine") and Paul's use of "the anger" for the final judgment in 2:5, 8 and 5:9. (2) The anger of the civil authority, as in 13:4-5 where the same word is used of the ruler's punishment. (3) The enemy's anger: give it room to cool by not answering back (a minority reading). The Plain keeps Paul's bare "the anger." See also the topic on wrath.
orig: δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ (dote topon tē orgē)

a: Vengeance is mine. I will pay back, says the Lord.
p: Paul's wording matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:35 exactly.
b: In the Song of Moses God says "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback" (Deuteronomy 32:35), words that came after God judged his own people as well as their enemies. Paul's phrase "I will pay back" differs from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint; the same wording appears in Hebrews 10:30, so many scholars think a form of the verse like this was already in circulation among Greek-speaking Jews and Christians. The law that forbids personal revenge makes the same point: "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people" (Leviticus 19:18). The book of Psalms also hands vengeance to God (Psalm 94:1). The idea is not that vengeance is good but that human beings are not its judges.

a: heap coals of fire on his head
p: Proverbs 25:22 gives the image; Christians have read it as shame, repentance, punishment or an Egyptian ritual.
b: Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 from the Greek, and stops before "the Lord will pay you back" (Proverbs 25:22: "you will be scooping up burning coals onto his head"). Readings: (1) Burning shame that may lead the enemy to repent; this has been the most common Christian reading and fits "overcome evil with good" (12:21). (2) Punishment: kindness increases the enemy's guilt before God, as coals are God's judgment in Psalm 140:10. This fits "Vengeance is mine" but sits oddly with doing good. (3) An Egyptian rite in which a penitent carried a pan of burning coals on his head (the view of Siegfried Morenz, supported by William Klassen), so that the coals are the enemy's repentance. (4) Kindled feelings of friendship. The Plain keeps the picture and leaves the meaning open.

a: must submit
p: Paul uses a word for taking one's place under someone, kept apart from 'obey'.
b: Hypotassō means to place oneself under or to line up beneath, and Paul uses it for a chosen attitude: wives to husbands (Ephesians 5:22, not yet written on this site), the church to Christ, and here believers to rulers. He does not use hypakouō, "obey," which he uses in 6:16-17 and 16:19 for obedience to God and to the gospel. The difference matters: one can accept a ruler's place and still refuse a command that God forbids, as Peter did: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). The Jewish community had long held that their rulers were set by God (Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 2:21; Wisdom 6:1-4) and had sought the good of the cities where they lived.
r: Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 2:21; Wisdom 6:1; Acts 5:29; Titus 3:1; 1 Peter 2:13

a: the authorities above them
p: Almost all read human rulers; a minority see spiritual powers behind them.
b: The Greek exousiai, "authorities," is the word Paul and his school also use for spiritual powers (1 Corinthians 15:24; Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:15). Oscar Cullmann, followed by Ernst Käsemann in part, argued that Paul means both: human rulers and the angelic powers who stand behind them. Most commentators reject that for 13:1-7, since the "authorities" here collect taxes (13:6) and "carry the sword" (13:4), and they take it as the Roman state and its officials, in Rome itself the emperor Nero (54-68) and his magistrates, but also local city councils and tax collectors throughout the empire. The Plain says only "the authorities above them" ("those who stand above," hyperechousai).

a: set in their places by God
p: Paul says God has 'set in place' rulers; he does not say that every act of a ruler is God's will.
b: Tetagmenai comes from taxis, order; the verb says God has put rulers in their rank, and 13:2 calls it "God's arrangement" (diatagē). The sentence is about the office, not about the approval of each ruler's conduct. Paul describes rulers as ideal in 13:3-4 (praising good, punishing evil), yet he had been beaten and jailed by Roman officials (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 16:22-24) and knew that his Lord had been executed by one. Elsewhere the Bible shows rulers who must be refused: the midwives who disobeyed Pharaoh (Exodus 1:17), Daniel's friends (Daniel 3:16-18), and the apostles (Acts 5:29). Revelation 13 shows a beast-state demanding worship. Christian traditions have drawn different limits; see the card.

a: will bring judgment on themselves
p: This passage has been used to defend rulers, to defend resisting rulers, and to condemn both.
b: Few verses in Paul have been used so differently. In 1750 the Boston minister Jonathan Mayhew preached that Romans 13 does not require submission to a tyrant; during the American Revolution Loyalist and Patriot preachers fought over the passage. In the 1800s it was cited for and against laws protecting slavery. In 1934 the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration limited the state's claim over the church, while some German pastors used Romans 13 to support the Nazi state. In 1985 the South African Kairos Document called an appeal to Romans 13 on behalf of the apartheid state "state theology." The card below gives what the churches teach.

a: It does not carry the sword for no reason.
p: 'The sword' stands for the right to punish with death, which Roman officials had.
b: The Greek machaira is a short sword. Roman governors had the "right of the sword" (ius gladii), the power to execute, and soldiers carried the weapon. Paul says the ruler does not bear it "for no reason" but as "an avenger to carry out anger" on wrongdoers. Christians have drawn different conclusions. Most churches teach that the state may use force in a just cause; the Anabaptist and Quaker traditions hold that the sword is "outside the perfection of Christ" (Schleitheim Confession, article 6) and that Christians should not carry it; see the card. Note that "servant" is diakonos, the word used of Christ in 15:8 and of Phoebe in 16:1.

a: for the sake of conscience
p: The Greek syneidesis is a person's inner awareness of right and wrong; here it is tied to God's order.
b: Syneidēsis, from "knowing with" oneself, is the inner witness to what one knows to be right or wrong. Paul speaks of conscience at 2:15 (the Gentiles' consciences "bear witness"), at 9:1 (Paul's own), and here. The sense is that submitting to authority is not just fear of punishment ("the anger") but a matter of seeing that the office is God's order. Later Christians made "conscience" a major concern: Luther before the Diet of Worms in 1521 said his conscience was captive to the word of God; the Westminster Confession (ch. 20) says God alone is lord of the conscience. See the topic on conscience.

a: This is also why you pay taxes.
p: Tacitus reports an outcry in Rome against tax collectors in AD 58, a year or two after Paul wrote.
b: Paul wrote in about 56 or 57. The Roman historian Tacitus reports that in AD 58 the people of Rome complained loudly against the tax farmers, who collected indirect taxes (customs and tolls) and were accused of abuse, and that the young emperor Nero thought of abolishing the taxes altogether; the senate persuaded him instead to publish the tax laws and curb the abuses (Annals 13.50-51). Some scholars (Moo, Dunn) think Paul already knew of a rising anger over taxes and wanted the Roman believers to stay out of any tax revolt. Others think the warning is general. Tax resistance was also in the air in Judea (it would break out in the revolt of AD 66). Jesus' saying about Caesar's coin is in Mark 12:17.

a: God's public servants
p: The Greek leitourgoi was used of civic officials and also of priests; Paul uses it of himself at 15:16.
b: Leitourgos was a word for a public official who served the community, often with his own money, and also for one who served in a temple. Paul uses it of the authorities here and of himself "as Christ Jesus' minister to the Gentiles" in 15:16, and it gives English "liturgy." The word shows that Paul does not think the tax collector's work is common or shameful: it is a service for God as well. He was not writing about an ideal state, since he tells the Romans in 12:19 that vengeance belongs to God and that earthly rulers are not the last judges.

a: If it is the tax, pay the tax. If it is the customs duty, pay the duty.
p: Paul names a direct tax (phoros) and an indirect one (telos).
b: Phoros was the tribute paid by subject peoples, on land and by head; telos covered customs, tolls and sales duties, usually collected by tax farmers (publicani), the group at the center of Tacitus' report (Annals 13.50-51). Paul covers both and adds two things that are not taxes: "respect" (phobos, fear of those with power to punish) and "honor" (timē). The order matters: Paul does not say to give a ruler's claims more than their due. Whether the emperor's claim to be honored as divine falls under "honor" is a question Christians in later years would face (Revelation 13).

a: Keep no debt hanging over anyone
p: He forbids leaving what is owed unpaid; the law allows loans.
b: The Greek opheilete is "owe." The verse has been used as a ban on all debt, and some Christians (for example, many Anabaptist and Brethren households) have lived by it. Most commentators read it as "pay what you owe when it is due," continuing 13:7, since the law of Moses allows and regulates lending (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7-8) and Paul says nothing against loans. Then he adds one debt that can never be paid off, the debt of love, using the same word he uses of his debt to Greeks and non-Greeks in 1:14 and the Gentiles' debt to Jerusalem in 15:27.

a: "Do not commit adultery,"
t: The order of the Ten Words
p: Paul puts adultery before murder, as the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 5 does.
b: The list is from the Ten Words: the Hebrew text of Exodus puts murder first, "You must not murder. You must not commit adultery. You must not steal" (Exodus 20:13-15). The Septuagint (in Codex Vaticanus) of Deuteronomy 5:17-19 puts adultery first, as Paul does; so do Philo (On the Decalogue), Luke 18:20 and James 2:11, while Mark 10:19 has murder first. Paul chooses the commands that concern neighbors and adds "and any other command." That does not mean the first four commands are dropped; love of neighbor is the second half of love of God.

a: You are to love your neighbor as yourself.
t: Leviticus 19:18, the summary of the law
p: Jewish teachers and Jesus both named this verse a summary of the law; Paul joins them.
b: In Leviticus the line closes a list of rules about how to treat others: "You are to love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:18). Rabbi Akiva (early 100s) called it "the great principle in the Torah" (Sifra, Qedoshim 4:12), and the earlier teacher Hillel gave the negative form, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary" (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Jesus named it the second great command (Mark 12:31). Paul uses it again at Galatians 5:14, and James calls it "the royal law" (James 2:8). In Leviticus "neighbor" is first of all a fellow Israelite; verse 34 extends the love to the foreigner living among them. Paul writes "the other person" in 13:8, with no limit.

a: love is the law fulfilled
p: Paul says love fulfills the law; he does not say the law is gone.
b: "Fulfilled" is the word of 8:4, where "the righteous requirement of the law" is "fulfilled in us." Paul's thought is that love is not an extra to the law nor a replacement, but what the law was always aiming at. For Jews, to love one's neighbor is not to leave the Torah's commands but to carry them out. Interpreters differ on what Paul means for Jewish believers who keep circumcision, Sabbath and food laws: the traditional Christian reading is that the ceremonial laws have been set aside and only the moral law remains; "Paul within Judaism" readers say Paul asks Gentiles to love their neighbors without being asked to keep the laws that mark Jews. See 14:14 and the cards on the Sabbath and food laws.

a: knowing what the moment is
p: Paul writes that salvation is nearer than when they first believed. What did he expect, and when?
b: Kairos is a moment of decision rather than clock time. "Salvation" here is the final rescue (compare 5:9-10; 8:23-24), which Paul sees as closer every day. Readings: (1) Paul expected Christ's return in his own lifetime or soon after, and the verse says so (the common historical reading; he says "we who are alive" in 1 Thessalonians 4:15). (2) He means a nearness that is always true; the final day gets closer every day for every believer, whenever it comes. (3) In the church year, Romans 13:11-14 was read on the first Sunday of Advent in the Roman rite, with Advent's mix of the Lord's coming in the past and still to come. The Church of England's 1662 Prayer Book uses 13:8-14 for the same Sunday.

a: weapons of light
p: The Greek hopla is weapons or gear for war; the light and darkness picture is common in Jewish writing.
b: Hopla is "weapons," and sometimes "armor." Paul uses the same word in 6:13 ("weapons of righteousness"; "tools" is also possible there) and builds the picture into the armor of God in Ephesians 6:11-17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8, where sleep, night and day are also used. The picture is of a soldier at dawn who throws off the clothes of the night and puts on his gear. The contrast of "sons of light" and "sons of darkness" runs through Jewish writings of this time, most clearly in the Qumran scroll called the War Scroll, and Paul's readers would hear it. The call to "wake up" ties to Jesus' teaching on being ready (Mark 13:35-37).

a: no drunken parties, no sleeping around and shameless living, no fighting and jealousy
p: Each pair joins an act to its fruit: parties and drink, sex and shamelessness, fights and jealousy.
b: Greek kōmoi were drunken processions through the streets at night, methai means drunkenness; koitai (literally "beds") means sexual excess, aselgeiai shameless, public acts; eris and zēlos are the quarrels that tore at churches (1 Corinthians 3:3). The three pairs move from the body to bed to the community. They also describe the night life of a big city. In 386 these were the words that Augustine read in a garden in Milan; see the note on 13:14.

a: Put on the Lord Jesus Christ
t: Putting on Christ, and Augustine's garden
p: The picture is of clothing, used in baptism; Augustine's conversion in 386 turned on this verse.
b: "Put on" (endysasthe) is the language of clothing, as in Galatians 3:27, "as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (see also Colossians 3:10-14). Many churches, from the early centuries, gave the newly baptized a white robe. In his Confessions (8.12), Augustine tells how in the summer of 386, sitting in a garden in Milan, he heard a child's voice chanting tolle lege, "take up and read," opened the book of Paul's letters and read the first passage he saw, Romans 13:13-14. In the Plain's own rendering of his Latin, "I did not want to read further, and there was no need." His account of his conversion shaped the Christian tradition's picture of grace in the West.

a: make arrangements for the flesh
p: Flesh is Paul's word for human life turned against God; 'make arrangements' means plan ahead.
b: Pronoia is "forethought," the planning one does ahead of time (for a journey, for a household). Paul says: do not plan for the flesh to get what it craves. "Flesh" (sarx) is the word Paul uses in 7:5 and 8:3-13 for human nature under the power of sin, not simply the body. It does not mean the body is bad. The point is to take away the occasion: not just resist when tempted but not arrange one's life to be tempted. Verse 14 is the last line of the exhortation that began at 12:1.

a: the one whose faith is weak
t: Who were the weak and the strong?
p: Paul never names them. Scholars have placed them in Rome's history in several ways.
b: Paul describes two groups. The "weak" eat only vegetables, keep certain days, and avoid wine (14:2, 5, 21); the "strong" (15:1) eat anything and treat all days alike. Views: (1) Jewish Christians who kept Torah food laws and Sabbaths, against Gentile Christians who did not (the traditional reading; but the Torah does not require vegetarianism or avoiding wine). (2) Jews and Gentiles who avoided meat and wine because it might have been offered to idols (the problem of 1 Corinthians 8 to 10). (3) A mixed group of scrupulous believers, including ascetics (Mark Reasoner). (4) Karl Donfried and A. J. M. Wedderburn tie the quarrel to the Jewish believers' return after Claudius' death, when they found Gentile believers in charge. (5) Mark Nanos argues the weak were Jews in the synagogue community, not Christ-believers. Paul's advice works for any of these: welcome without judging.

a: eats only vegetables
p: Jews in Gentile settings sometimes ate only vegetables to avoid food that was not clean or had been offered to idols.
b: Daniel and his friends asked for vegetables and water in the king's court (Daniel 1:8-16), and the book of Tobit says Tobit refused to eat the Gentiles' food in exile (Tobit 1:10-11). Josephus, in his Life (13-14), reports that priests he knew who were taken to Rome as prisoners lived on figs and nuts so as not to defile themselves with the food of their captors. A believer in Rome who could not be sure whether the butcher's meat had come from a pagan temple might have done the same. The Torah does not command vegetarianism; this is a safe practice, not the law.

a: a household slave who belongs to someone else
t: Household slave, and who the master is
p: Paul's picture is one of a slave with another master; 'the Lord' here is Christ.
b: Oiketēs is a slave in a household. Paul's picture: another person's slave is not yours to judge; his master will decide whether he does well or badly. Paul's 'Who are you?' echoes his earlier rebuke to the interlocutor in 2:1 and 9:20, and James 4:12 uses the same language. The "Lord" is Christ (14:9). The Byzantine text reads "God" here; see the textual note.

a: One person judges one day to stand above another
p: Paul does not say which days; the Sabbath is the likeliest, along with fast days and festivals.
b: Candidates: (1) the Sabbath and Jewish festivals (the most common reading; compare Galatians 4:10 and Colossians 2:16); (2) fast days, such as the Monday and Thursday fasts that Jews and the Didache's "hypocrites" kept, against the Wednesday and Friday fasts of the Didache (Didache 8.1); (3) days thought lucky or unlucky in Roman custom. Paul asks only that each be fully sure; neither side is wrong. The Sabbath is a command of the Torah for Jews, and Paul never says that Jews should stop keeping it. How churches have read the Sabbath since is the subject of the card below. See Acts 20:7 for the Christian meeting "on the first day of the week."

a: gives thanks to God
p: Eater and non-eater both thank God: that is Paul's test.
b: Jews said a blessing before eating, a practice laid out in Mishnah Berakhot 6 and followed by Jesus (Mark 6:41), and Paul takes it for granted. He does not ask what each person eats but whether he can thank God for it and do it "for the Lord." Compare 1 Corinthians 10:30-31 and 1 Timothy 4:3-5. The Byzantine text adds a line about the person who does not keep the day; see the textual note.

a: We will all stand in front of God's judgment seat.
p: Paul wrote from Corinth, where the judge's platform stood in the market.
b: The bēma was the raised platform on which a Roman official sat to hear cases. Paul had stood before the bēma of Gallio at Corinth: "led him before the judgment seat" (Acts 18:12). Paul writes from that city, and the Corinthian bēma, a large raised stone platform in the forum, is visible there today. In 2 Corinthians 5:10 he says "we must all appear before Christ's judgment seat." Here the oldest text says "God's," and later copies read "Christ's." That the judge is God removes every human claim to judge a brother.

a: every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will confess to God
p: Paul's 'As I live, says the Lord' replaces Isaiah's oath; Philippians 2:10-11 applies the same verse to Jesus.
b: In Isaiah 45:23 God says "I have taken an oath by myself; ... every knee will bend before me; every tongue will take its oath" (Isaiah 45:23). Paul's opening, "As I live, says the Lord," is a stock oath formula of the prophets (Numbers 14:28; Ezekiel 5:11), not a line from this verse. The Greek verb he uses, exomologēsetai, means "will confess" or "will give praise"; the Septuagint has it in Isaiah. The same verse is applied to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11, which is not yet written on this site. Here, "the Lord" and "God" are both used of the judge.

a: nothing is common in itself
p: The word koinos (common) is the one in Peter's vision; Paul says nothing is common 'in itself'.
b: Paul writes koinos, "common," which in Jewish usage meant ordinary, not set apart for God, and so unfit to eat. It is the word of Peter's vision: "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (Acts 10:15). Mark's narrator says of Jesus' teaching, "With this he made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Paul writes that he is "convinced in the Lord Jesus." Readings: (1) the traditional Christian reading, that Paul sets aside the food laws of Leviticus 11 for all believers; (2) Paul is speaking to the strong about the conscience of the weak, and says nothing about what Jews who follow Jesus should do (a common reading among those who read Paul within Judaism, such as Mark Nanos and Paula Fredriksen); (3) he states a principle (nothing is unclean in itself) while allowing different practices. See the card.

a: The kingdom of God is not food and drink.
t: The kingdom of God in Romans
p: This is the only time Romans names the kingdom of God; Paul defines it by what the Spirit gives.
b: Paul uses "the kingdom of God" only a few times (1 Corinthians 4:20; 6:9-10; 15:50; Galatians 5:21), always in letters to churches that need to remember what it is about. Here it is not a set of rules about food and days but "righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Righteousness may mean right relations among people (the word is used of God in 1:17), peace is what 14:19 pursues, and joy comes from the Spirit. Jesus' own sayings about what goes in and what comes out (Mark 7:15-23) stand behind the point.

a: drink wine
p: Wine and meat might have been poured out or offered to idols; Paul's examples are likely the weak's worries.
b: Sellers at the market might have received their meat from a pagan temple, and wine was poured out as an offering at public meals and many private ones. A Jew or a Gentile convert concerned about idols might refuse both. Paul addresses the same worry in 1 Corinthians 8:1-13 and 10:25-29 (not yet written on this site). Daniel refused the king's wine (Daniel 1:8). Paul has not said the strong must never eat meat; he says they should refuse it, if the weak person's faith would be wounded. "It is good" (kalon) is gentle.

a: not done out of faith
p: Paul means acting against one's own conviction; later writers used the verse for the doctrine of sin.
b: In context pistis here is conviction: eating while believing it wrong. A person who eats against conscience does wrong even if the food is clean. In the later church, the line was read more widely. Augustine used it to argue that the virtues of those without faith in Christ fall short of God; Article 13 of the Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles says works done before grace "have the nature of sin." The Council of Trent condemned the claim that all works before justification are sins (session 6, canon 7). Most modern commentators read it only for the conscience of the weak and strong.

a: The insults of those who insult you fell on me.
p: Paul hears Christ speaking in the Psalm: he took on the insults aimed at God.
b: In Psalm 69:9 the psalmist says "Zeal for your house has eaten me up, for the insults of those who insult you have landed on me" (Psalm 69:9). The Gospels use the first half of the verse of Jesus in the temple (John 2:17), and Paul uses the second half here. The Messiah's mind: he put others first, even to bearing insults meant for God. The text applies the principle of 15:1-2: the strong should bear with the weak, as Christ bore what was not his. Psalm 69 is among the most cited psalms in the New Testament.

a: All that was put in writing in earlier days was put in writing to instruct us
p: A Jewish writer tells a largely Gentile audience that the Hebrew Scriptures were written for them too.
b: By "all that was put in writing in earlier days" Paul means the Scriptures of Israel, the only Bible he and the Roman churches had. He tells them that these writings, which were given to Israel, were also written "to instruct us," and the next verses show it with four quotations. This is typical of Paul (compare 1 Corinthians 10:11). Jewish readers will notice the claim that texts given to Israel instruct Gentiles. It sets the stage for 15:8-12, where the Scriptures give both Jews and Gentiles a reason to praise God together.

a: a servant of the circumcised
t: Christ the servant of the circumcised
p: Christ's service to Jews confirms God's promises to the patriarchs, and so opens the way for the nations to praise God.
b: "The circumcised" means the Jewish people. Paul says Christ became their servant "to show God's truth" by making the promises to the patriarchs firm. Christ himself says, "I have not been sent to anyone but the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (Matthew 15:24). Gentile mercy follows (15:9), but it is not a replacement: the Gentiles' praise rests on God keeping his word to Israel. This is a key text for those who reject the idea that the church replaced Israel (supersessionism). The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate 4 draws on Romans 9 to 11, and N. T. Wright and James Dunn both read 15:8-9 as the ending of the whole argument. Compare 3:1-4; 9:4-5; 11:28-29.

a: For this reason I will give you thanks among the Gentiles, and make music to your name.
p: The speaker in the Psalm is David, praising among the nations; Paul hears Christ praising among the Gentiles.
b: In Psalm 18:49 the king says "That is why I will give you thanks among the nations, LORD; to your name I will make music" (Psalm 18:49; it is also in 2 Samuel 22:50). In the Psalm David thanks God for victory, in the presence of the nations he defeated. Paul hears a larger voice, that of the Messiah who praises God among the Gentiles, through the church, joined by "his people" (15:10). Paul's quotation follows the Greek, with "Gentiles" for the Hebrew goyim (nations).

a: Be glad, you Gentiles, together with his people.
p: The line comes from the end of the Song of Moses, where the Greek Bible has the nations rejoicing with Israel.
b: Paul quotes the Septuagint's line "Rejoice, nations, with his people" from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:43). The Hebrew text has a harder line with the same words "nations" and "his people." The longer form found at Qumran and in the Greek adds the heavens and the gods bowing down to God, which is the form this site's Plain of Deuteronomy 32:43 follows; see the notes there. This is the only quotation in the chain from the Torah, and it comes at the end of a song that was largely a warning to Israel. The word "together" gives the point: Gentiles do not replace Israel, they join it.

a: There will be the root of Jesse
t: Isaiah 11:10 and the chain of four quotations
p: Four quotations from the Torah, Prophets and Psalms close the argument with the nations praising God.
b: The chain is Psalm 18:49 (15:9), Deuteronomy 32:43 (15:10), Psalm 117:1 (15:11) and Isaiah 11:10 (15:12). Each has "Gentiles" or "peoples." The first two have Gentiles with Jews; the second two Gentiles alone. Psalm 117:1 reads "All you nations, praise the LORD! All you peoples, applaud him!" (Psalm 117:1). Isaiah 11:10 in this site's Plain reads "nations will come seeking him" (Isaiah 11:10); Paul quotes the Greek version, "the Gentiles will hope in him." The Hebrew verb is "seek" (darash), the Greek "hope." Isaiah 11 is the passage about the shoot from Jesse's stump, which Christians read of Jesus as Messiah. Paul ends his case by placing Gentile praise in the Scripture's own words.

a: doing a priest's work for the good news of God
t: Paul as priest, Gentiles as offering
p: Paul uses temple language of himself; the Gentiles are the offering, an idea from Isaiah 66.
b: "Minister" is leitourgos and "doing a priest's work" is hierourgeō, from hiereus, priest; "offering" (prosphora) and "made holy" complete the picture. Paul is not a priest by descent, and he uses the language as a picture of his work of preaching. The offering is the Gentiles themselves, an idea close to Isaiah 66:20: "They will bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD" (Isaiah 66:20). Isaiah 66:19 speaks of survivors sent to Tarshish, which some scholars (James Scott) identify with Spain, Paul's next goal (15:24).

a: from Jerusalem and around in a circle as far as Illyricum
p: Paul describes a great arc around the eastern Mediterranean; Illyricum is the farthest point.
b: Illyricum was a Roman province on the east side of the Adriatic (today Croatia and Albania), reached by the Egnatian Road from Macedonia. Acts says nothing of a mission there; Acts 20:2 reports only that Paul "came to Greece." Paul may have gone there from Macedonia during the stay behind Acts 20:1-2. "Completed" here cannot mean that everyone had heard; he means he has planted churches in the main cities (Antioch, Ephesus, Thessalonica, Corinth) along the arc, so no more room is left "in these regions" (15:23).

a: where Christ has not yet been named
t: Not building on another's foundation, and who founded the Roman church
p: Paul says he plants churches only where Christ is unknown; Rome's church was not his, and no one knows who founded it.
b: Paul has never visited Rome, and the Roman church was not founded by an apostle that we know. The fourth-century writer called Ambrosiaster says the Romans came to faith through Jews who had visited Jerusalem, without seeing signs. The Jewish community of Rome had links to Jerusalem (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome), and Suetonius' report of disturbances over "Chrestus" in about AD 49 (see Acts 18:2) is read by many as the church's first trace. Later tradition says Peter and Paul both died in Rome (1 Clement 5:4); Paul does not name Peter in the greetings of chapter 16. This is why Paul calls his visit a passing stop on the way to Spain (15:24), not a mission.

a: Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.
p: The line is from the fourth servant song; Paul takes it as a motto for first-time hearers.
b: In Isaiah 52:15 God says kings will see "what no one had told them, and understand what they had never heard" (Isaiah 52:15). Paul quotes the Greek version, which adds "about him" and so points the line to the Messiah, and applies it to peoples who had never heard of Christ. The same part of Isaiah supplies the feet of the messenger who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7, quoted at Romans 10:15) and the question of Isaiah 53:1 (quoted at Romans 10:16). He is, again, claiming the Servant's own task of reaching the nations.

a: Spain
t: Why Spain, and did Paul get there?
p: Spain was the far west of the Roman world; whether Paul went is uncertain.
b: Hispania was a Latin-speaking part of the empire with a large Roman population. By going there, Paul would be carrying the good news to "the end of the earth" as his generation measured it, which fits his reading of Isaiah's mission to the nations. He asks Rome for support, "sent on" (propempō) with guides, money and letters, as in Titus 3:13. Did he go? 1 Clement 5:7 says Paul reached "the limit of the west," which may mean Spain or Rome; the Muratorian Fragment says he left Rome for Spain; the Acts of Peter tells of his going. Acts ends in Rome and says nothing of Spain, and the Pastoral Letters, if his, imply later travel in the east. Whether he went is unknown.

a: to serve the saints
p: Paul's gift from the Gentile churches for the poor of Jerusalem was a major project of his later years.
b: The project is described in Galatians 2:10, 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 and 2 Corinthians 8 to 9 (none yet written on this site). Paul had agreed to "remember the poor," and now brings the gift. His reasons: need (the Jerusalem church was poor), thanks (15:27), and unity of Gentile and Jewish believers. Some scholars (Johannes Munck) see a picture of Isaiah's vision of the nations bringing their wealth to Zion; Leander Keck argues "the poor" was a title the Jerusalem church used for itself. Paul expected danger (15:31). Acts mentions the gift only once and in passing, when Paul says he came "to give alms for my people and to present offerings" (Acts 24:17), and Acts 20:4 lists delegates traveling with him.

a: they owe it to them
p: The Gentile churches share in Israel's spiritual blessings, and so owe material help.
b: The word is again opheiletai, "owe" (13:8). Paul's logic is about reciprocity: the spiritual blessings of Israel (9:4-5) came to Gentiles through Jews; so Gentiles repay with gifts. It is the practical side of the olive-tree image of 11:17-24, where the wild branch is warned not to boast against the root. This verse is a favorite of those who stress the Gentiles' debt to Israel; compare the topic on the church and Israel.

a: safe and sealed
p: The verb sphragizo means to seal; Paul may mean putting the gift safely in their hands.
b: Sphragizō is to seal with a stamp. Readings: (1) deliver the money intact in a sealed bag; (2) certify that the gift is a true fruit of Gentile faith; (3) secure it for Jerusalem as a done deal. The "fruit" is the collection. In 15:31 Paul fears it may not be accepted.

a: those in Judea who refuse to believe
p: The Greek can mean unbelieving Jews or the disobedient; Paul fears both opposition outside and doubt inside.
b: Apeitheō is "disobey, refuse to be persuaded," and elsewhere in Romans it is used for Israel's refusal (10:21; 11:30-31). Paul asks prayer to be rescued from them. His second request, that the gift be "acceptable to the saints," shows he also feared the Jerusalem believers might not take it. Acts reports both threats: Jews from Asia seized him in the temple (Acts 21:27-28), and the elders warned him of rumors: "But they have been told things about you" (Acts 21:21). Paul arrived in Jerusalem and was taken into custody; Acts does not say if the gift was accepted. The Plain follows the plain sense.

a: servant of the church in Cenchreae
p: Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae; the same word means deacon elsewhere.
b: Diakonos is a "servant" and Paul uses it for Christ (15:8), the ruler (13:4), himself and Apollos (1 Corinthians 3:5). It is also the church office, as in Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8-13. With "of the church in Cenchreae" many commentators (Cranfield, Dunn, Jewett) think Paul names a recognized role, and Origen, in his commentary (in Rufinus' Latin), took this as proof that women were set apart for ministry in the church. The word "deaconess" is a later coinage. Others hold that Paul uses an everyday sense, "one who serves," without an office. The Plain keeps "servant." Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth, excavated in the 1960s and 1970s. The churches differ on women's ordination; see the card at 16:7.

a: Let me recommend to you Phoebe
p: Phoebe almost certainly carried the letter to Rome; this is a letter of recommendation for her.
b: Chapter 16 opens like a Greek letter of recommendation (compare 2 Corinthians 3:1): the writer introduces the bearer and asks for help. Since Paul sends no other courier, most scholars (Jewett, Dunn) conclude that Phoebe carried the letter to Rome, as the later subscript in many manuscripts says, "written to the Romans from Corinth by Phoebe." A letter bearer often read it aloud and explained it, so she may have been its first interpreter. This depends on the likeliest reading of 16:1-2; the text does not say it outright. The subscriptions are later additions, not Paul's.

a: She has been a patron to many people
p: A prostatis was a patron, a person of means who helped others; Paul says Phoebe helped even him.
b: Prostatis is the feminine of prostatēs, patron. In Roman society a patron gave money, housing, legal protection and introductions to clients. Women patrons are known in inscriptions; at Corinth, in the middle of the first century, a woman named Junia Theodora was honored by Lycian cities for her help, according to inscriptions (reported by Bruce Winter). Phoebe was likely a woman of means. Paul, who often says he refuses support, accepts that he has been helped by her. The word is from the same root as "the one who leads" in 12:8. Her request is not charity but business: "whatever business she needs."

a: Prisca and Aquila
t: Prisca and Aquila, back in Rome
p: Paul's coworkers had been forced out of Rome by Claudius; their return to Rome and his greeting fix the date.
b: Acts calls her Priscilla, a pet form; Paul always uses Prisca. In Acts 18:2 Luke says that Aquila and Priscilla had left Rome "since Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome," which Suetonius (Claudius 25.4) reports in a form that suggests riots over "Chrestus," probably about AD 49. They met Paul in Corinth, went with him to Ephesus (Acts 18:18-19; 1 Corinthians 16:19), and by the time of this letter had returned to Rome, perhaps after Claudius died in 54, and hosted a church in their house (16:5). They are named first (as in four of the six times they appear together), and Paul calls them "fellow workers," a title he also gives Timothy and Urbanus (16:9, 21).

a: They risked their own necks to save my life.
p: The picture is of putting one's neck under the sword; the occasion is unknown.
b: The Greek ton heautōn trachēlon hypethēkan is "put their own necks under," an image of the executioner's block. When it happened is not known. Ephesus is the likeliest place (Acts 19:23-41; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8-10), since they were there with Paul. Paul says that "all the churches of the Gentiles" thank them, so their act helped a mission beyond Paul's own.

a: the church that meets in their house
p: Chapter 16 names at least five groups; none is a church building.
b: The first Christians had no church buildings. Paul greets, besides Prisca and Aquila's house church, "those from the household of Aristobulus" (16:10), "those from the household of Narcissus" (16:11), "the brothers with" five named men (16:14), and "all the saints" with five other people (16:15). That is five or more groups. Peter Lampe, studying the sites and names, argues that Roman Christians met in scattered apartments and workshops, with no single bishop over them. The house church of Prisca and Aquila is also found in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19). Hosting a church was a work of the patron (16:2).

a: Epaenetus
t: Epaenetus, and the argument over chapter 16
p: A man from Asia is greeted in Rome; the long greeting list led some to think this chapter was sent to Ephesus.
b: "The firstfruits of Asia" (Asia was the Roman province with Ephesus as its capital) would be the first convert there. Why would Paul know twenty-odd people in a city he had never visited? T. W. Manson and others (1948) proposed that chapter 16 was a note for Ephesus, where Prisca and Aquila and Epaenetus had lived. Against this: travel in the empire was constant, Rome drew people from everywhere (and returning exiles, like Prisca and Aquila), and Paul has no other way to claim his link with the Roman church than to name those he knows. Harry Gamble (1977) argued that the chapter belongs to the letter, and most scholars agree. Some details do not need Ephesus: "the household of Aristobulus" and "Narcissus" point to Rome. See the chapter commentary.

a: Mary
p: Paul uses the verb for hard labor of Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis, the verb he uses of his own work.
b: The Greek verb kopiaō means to work to exhaustion. Paul uses it for his own work as an apostle (1 Corinthians 15:10; Galatians 4:11) and for church leaders (1 Thessalonians 5:12). He applies it to four women in the chapter: Mary (16:6), Tryphaena and Tryphosa (16:12) and Persis (16:12). Mary's name is the Jewish Miriam. Of the 25 people named in 16:1 to 16:15 (including Phoebe) eight are women. The kind of work is not stated.

a: Andronicus and Junia
p: Ancient readers took the name as a woman's, Junia; from the Middle Ages some made it a man, Junias.
b: The Greek Iounian is the accusative of a name that could be Junia (a woman; the common Latin name) or Junias (a man; a short form of Junianus). No ancient inscription or text outside this verse is known to use "Junias" as a man's name; it appears only in late lists that make Junias a male bishop, which Epp and Lampe discuss. Lampe allows that "Junias" could be a short form of the man's name Junianus, but notes how rare the evidence is. Junia, by contrast, is a common name for women in Rome (Peter Lampe counted over 250 examples). The church fathers who comment on the verse, Chrysostom among them, take it as a woman, and Chrysostom marvels that a woman was counted worthy of the title of apostle. Origen (in Rufinus' Latin) has been read both ways. A masculine "Junias" enters later, in the Middle Ages, and it was printed in the Greek text of NA26 (1979) as Iounian with a circumflex; NA27 (1993) and later returned to the feminine accent. Andronicus and Junia were probably a married couple; the Greek name Andronicus is common.

a: They are outstanding among the apostles
t: 'Outstanding among the apostles' or 'well known to the apostles'?
p: The Greek can mean they were apostles, or that the apostles knew them well.
b: The words are episēmoi en tois apostolois. The issue is the phrase en + plural dative. (1) "Outstanding among the apostles": Andronicus and Junia were themselves apostles, a wider group than the Twelve (1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 1:19; Acts 14:14). This was the reading of the Greek fathers and is held by Eldon Epp, Linda Belleville and most recent commentators. (2) "Well known to the apostles": they were respected by the apostles but were not apostles themselves. Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace argued in 2001 that Greek usage supports this; Epp and Belleville replied with other Greek texts (for example Psalms of Solomon 2:6). "Apostle" here would mean someone sent as a missionary, not necessarily one of the Twelve. Paul says they were "in Christ before I was," so they were among the earliest believers; where and when they joined is not stated (some suppose Jerusalem, soon after Easter, but that is a guess).
r: 1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 1:19; Acts 14:14; Psalms of Solomon 2:6

a: those from the household of Aristobulus
p: These are slaves or freed people of powerful households; Paul does not greet the masters.
b: A "household" was the family, the slaves and the freed people of a master. J. B. Lightfoot suggested that the Aristobulus was a grandson of Herod the Great who lived in Rome and whose slaves passed to the emperor, forming "Aristobuliani" (not certain). Narcissus (16:11) is often identified as Claudius' powerful freedman secretary, who was forced to die in AD 54, soon after Nero came to power (Tacitus, Annals 13.1), and whose household then passed to the emperor. Paul greets "those who are in the Lord," not the masters, who were perhaps not believers or no longer alive. The identification is a guess, in both cases.

a: Tryphaena and Tryphosa
t: Names that suggest slaves and freed people
p: Many of the names in the greeting list were common among slaves and freed people at Rome.
b: "Tryphaena" and "Tryphosa" are from tryphē (delicate, luxurious); they may be sisters. Persis means "Persian woman." Hermes, Patrobas, Nereus, Julia, Ampliatus, Urbanus and Philologus are all names found among slaves and freed persons in Rome's inscriptions, including imperial households (Lampe). A man named Ampliatus appears in a tomb inscription in a Roman catacomb, and Patrobas has been compared with Nero's freedman Patrobius (Tacitus, Histories 1.49), but such identifications are guesses, since the names were common. The picture is of a church of working people with a few of means, matching the picture in Paul's other letters.

a: Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother
t: Rufus and Simon of Cyrene's family
p: Mark names a Rufus as son of the man who carried Jesus' cross; some think this is the same man.
b: Mark says Simon of Cyrene, who was drafted to carry the cross, was "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21). Mark's naming of the sons suggests that his readers knew them, and church tradition connects Mark with Rome. If this is the same Rufus, his mother (Simon's wife) had cared for Paul at some time, as Paul calls her "a mother to me also." It is a possibility, not proven: Rufus was a common Latin name. "Chosen" (eklektos) may be a plain title of believers or mean "outstanding."

a: holy kiss
p: A kiss of greeting among believers; it became the kiss of peace in worship.
b: Paul commands a "holy kiss" at the end of four letters (also 1 Corinthians 16:20; 2 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Thessalonians 5:26), and 1 Peter 5:14 calls it a "kiss of love." In the ancient world the kiss on the cheek or mouth greeted family and friends. In Justin's account of worship in Rome around AD 150, the congregation greeted one another with a kiss after the prayers (First Apology 65). The kiss of peace remains in the liturgies of the Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches, and some Anabaptist and Brethren groups still practice an actual kiss among members. It marks the church as one family across lines of rank.

a: stir up divisions
p: The warning interrupts the greetings; some scholars think it was added, though all the manuscripts have it.
b: After warm greetings the tone suddenly changes, and Paul names no opponents or errors. This has led some scholars (Robert Jewett, among others) to call 16:17-20 a later insertion. Against that: every manuscript of Romans has it, Paul often interrupts himself (Philippians 3:2; 1 Corinthians 16:22), and "divisions" and "stumbling blocks" recall the quarrels of 14:1 to 15:13 (the word "stumbling block" is the one in 14:13). Who the troublemakers were is not said: they could be a group of those pressing Gentile Christians to keep the law, or boastful teachers, or the strong and weak themselves. "Steer clear" is the opposite of Paul's earlier advice to welcome everyone. The Plain reads the passage as Paul's.

a: their own bellies
p: A common Greek insult for self-indulgent people; some see a dig at food-law quarrels.
b: "Serving the belly" was a standard Greek insult for people ruled by appetite (compare Philippians 3:19, "their god is their belly"). Most commentators take it as general self-seeking, with "smooth words and flattering talk" as the means. A few have wondered if Paul is jabbing at those who made food the center of the faith (14:1-23). "Our Lord Christ" is the reading of the early manuscripts; later ones read "our Lord Jesus Christ."

a: crush Satan under your feet
p: Paul seems to echo the promise that the woman's offspring will strike the serpent's head.
b: God's words to the serpent in Eden were "He will strike you on the head" (Genesis 3:15). The language of "crush ... under your feet" may echo that verse, and Jewish and Christian interpreters read it of the Messiah's victory, as in the Aramaic Targum Pseudo-Jonathan. It is the only mention of Satan in Romans. "The God of peace" will do it, not the believers, and the believers' feet are the instrument. Luke 10:19 and Psalm 91:13 use the same picture. The Plain ends the verse with Paul's usual grace; the Byzantine text adds "Christ" (see the textual note).

a: Timothy, my fellow worker
p: The names match Acts' list of Paul's companions at the end of his stay in Greece.
b: Timothy is Paul's closest helper (Acts 16:1). Lucius, Jason and Sosipater are "relatives," meaning fellow Jews (see 9:3). A Jason was Paul's host at Thessalonica (Acts 17:5-9), and Sosipater may be the Sopater of Berea in Acts 20:4. The Acts text says that Paul "stayed three months" in Greece (Acts 20:3), which is when most date Romans. A Lucius of Cyrene appears in Acts 13:1, and Origen thought this Lucius was Luke; the Greek name differs, and "relative" points to a Jew. All are sure to have been men Paul trusted.

a: Tertius, the one who wrote this letter down
t: The scribe who adds his own greeting
p: Letters like Romans were dictated to a scribe; Tertius is the only one who names himself.
b: Paul dictated his letters and signed at the end (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11). Tertius ("third," a common Latin slave name) breaks in with his own greeting. Scribes in Paul's time sometimes had freedom to shape wording; E. Randolph Richards studied the practice and concluded that Paul's letters may reflect more of their style than assumed, and that the length and carefulness of Romans fit a skilled scribe. "In the Lord" may go with his greeting or with his writing.

a: Erastus, the city treasurer
t: Erastus of Corinth and the pavement inscription
p: A Latin inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paid for a pavement; whether he is Paul's friend is debated.
b: Paul's word is oikonomos tēs poleōs, an official in charge of a city's money. A slab found in 1929 near the theater at Corinth carries the Latin words Erastus pro aedilitate s(ua) p(ecunia) stravit, "Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for the aedileship." Henry Cadbury and Gerd Theissen argued that the two are the same man, who rose from treasurer to aedile. Others point out that the Latin title (aedile) and Paul's Greek title (a lower office, in the view of some) do not match, and Erastus was a common name. It is often cited, but is not proven. Acts 19:22 names an Erastus among Paul's helpers, and 2 Timothy 4:20 an Erastus at Corinth.

a: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church
p: Gaius had a house large enough for the Corinthian church, or hosted travelers.
b: Paul baptized a Gaius in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14). If this is the same man, his house was where Paul stayed and where the "whole church" could meet, or the host of all traveling Christians. Some think he is the Titius Justus of Acts 18:7, whose house was next to the synagogue, since Gaius could be his first name. This is a guess. A house able to hold the whole church of a major city suggests a man of some means.

a: the unveiling of the mystery kept in silence for long ages
p: The 'mystery' is the long-hidden plan of God, now made known: Gentiles join in the promise.
b: "Mystery" (mystērion) in Paul means a divine plan once hidden and now revealed (11:25; Colossians 1:26-27; Ephesians 3:3-9, not yet written on this site). In Daniel 2 the "mystery" is what God shows the king. Here it is God's plan, silent in earlier ages, to bring the Gentiles into the people of God by Christ. But the next verse says it is made known "through the writings of the prophets," so it was hidden in plain sight, in the Scriptures, until Christ opened them (compare 1:2; 3:21). The doxology puts "my good news" next to the "preaching of Jesus Christ," meaning probably the preaching about him and by him.

a: to lead them to the obedience of faith
t: 'The obedience of faith', the letter's frame
p: The phrase returns from 1:5, closing the letter as it opened.
b: The same phrase, hypakoē pisteōs, opens the letter (1:5) and closes it here; this is called an inclusio, a frame. See the note at 1:5 for the three readings (obedience that is faith; obedience that flows from faith; the obedience that faith gives). "All the Gentiles" (panta ta ethnē) also recalls 1:5, "all the Gentiles." The frame is one reason why some commentators hold that the doxology was written by Paul or by someone who knew the letter well; those who doubt its origin point to the same echoes as signs of an imitator.

a: to the only wise God
t: 'The only wise God' and the sentence's grammar
p: The phrase is also found in 1 Timothy and Jude; the sentence ends awkwardly.
b: "The only God" is a Jewish confession (Deuteronomy 6:4); "the only wise God" appears also in some copies of 1 Timothy 1:17 and in Jude 25 (as a related phrase). The sentence which began in 16:25 ("Now to the one...") never finishes smoothly: it ends "to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory," where "to whom" refers back in an awkward way. This grammar is one of the reasons some doubt that the doxology came from Paul's pen; others see an elevated style typical of liturgy. Commentators note the clumsy "to whom," and copyists seem to have tried to smooth it.
